extracted.intended_audience: readers of philosophical aphorisms; students and scholars of Pascal; general readers interested in human nature and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Pascal's numbered aphorisms (Pensees) offering principles and observations about power, custom, justice, reason, scepticism, human greatness and misery. Useful for analyzing or teaching Pascal's reflections on human nature and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cords of necessity bind respect
rubrics_metrics.description: The social bonds that make people respect one another are generally cords of necessity: hierarchy arises because not all can rule, so necessity creates degrees and ties of respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues imagine society forming: conflict yields a dominant party, which then institutionalizes power (election, heredity). These institutional forms are sustained by necessity and by imagination; respect is rooted in practical necessity before being mystified by custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power becomes sustained by imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Once force determines power, imagination and opinion sustain it: institutions (nobility, burgesses) and rites give continued legitimacy beyond raw might.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After dominance is settled by force, the ruling group's imagination builds legitimizing practices (ceremony, titles) that make authority appear natural rather than contingent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between real power and imagined rank
rubrics_metrics.description: Some offices (kings) have real power independent of imagination; others (chancellors, judges, physicians) largely appeal to imagination and ceremony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External trappings (guards, drums, robes) create an imaginative force that makes persons command respect even when the underlying power differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom determines justice
rubrics_metrics.description: As custom decides what is agreeable, custom also determines what is called 'justice'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established laws are regarded as just because they are established; this shows justice is socially constituted rather than inherently self-evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of government: opinion and might
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments founded on opinion and imagination are pleasant and voluntary but temporary; governments founded on might last forever. 'Opinion is queen; might is tyrant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrast highlights the fragility of legitimacy grounded only in consent/opinion versus brute force's durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as established law (conventionalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is what is established by society; therefore our established laws will be regarded as just without examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This asserts a conventionalist view: legitimacy attaches to what is accepted, making critical claims about the possibility of objective justice within customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil wars follow attempts to reward desert
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil wars are the greatest evil and are inevitable if society attempts to reward desert precisely, since everyone will claim merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal suggests social peace sometimes requires arbitrary, indisputable criteria (e.g., hereditary succession) to avoid conflict over merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom is a force that compels outward respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom enforces actions (e.g., saluting a man in brocade) by social sanction; habit makes us attribute natural authority to outward signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people expect to salute a richly dressed person because custom would punish noncompliance; habit leads the world to believe such respect is natural rather than constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superficial signs indicate social power
rubrics_metrics.description: Being well-dressed or 'spruce' signals that many people serve you; external splendour is a visible indicator of power, not mere vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal defends outward signs as practical markers of resources (valet, perfumer, lace) that materially increase one's capabilities ('the more arms one has, the more powerful one is').

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference as socially costly signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference means putting oneself to inconvenience to show one would do so for others if needed; that cost distinguishes the great from ordinary people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because deference requires real inconvenience, it serves as a credible, differentiating social signal—if everyone deferred cheaply, no distinction would result.

rubrics_metrics.name: External markers settle precedence and prevent conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: We use external, countable indicators (e.g., number of lackeys) to determine precedence to avoid quarrels over personal merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues this arbitrary ordering serves peace: accepting visible signs of rank is rational given human dispositions toward conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary succession as practical solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing the eldest son as ruler is absurd by reason but practical because it avoids civil war; clarity and indisputability maintain order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal emphasizes the trade-off: justice by merit would provoke endless disputes, so simple rules (birth order) reduce costly conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: We love people for their qualities, not their selves
rubrics_metrics.description: Love is directed at perishable qualities (beauty, judgment), not an immutable ego; thus honouring rank is consistent with loving borrowed qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undermines romantic ideas of loving the 'self' and explains social deference to status as attachment to visible, influential traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular opinions are often sound in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Common people’s preferences (e.g., diversion over poetry; valuing external marks; being offended by a blow; seeking glory) are reasonable for reasons that the half-learned miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal lists concrete examples to show folk wisdom has practical rationales rooted in human life and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow custom because it is custom (authority of acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom should be followed simply because it is customary; people follow it because they think it just, but the proper basis is authority and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If people acknowledged that laws are only authoritative because they are laws, they would avoid revolting when philosophical arguments show them to be valueless; but people believe laws are true, not only authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of denouncing laws as unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: It is dangerous to tell people that laws are unjust, because they obey them only insofar as they believe them just; therefore, to prevent sedition, teach obedience to law as law rather than appeal solely to justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical political counsel: couch obedience in terms of duty to lawful superiors, not in contested moral judgments, to maintain order.

rubrics_metrics.name: The world judges well in its natural ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary world (people and the truly wise who return to a 'learned ignorance') often judges better than the semi-learned who have some vain knowledge and pretend wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal distinguishes three epistemic positions—natural ignorance, learned ignorance, and the half-knowledge that misleads—arguing that popular judgment is often reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation and dialectic of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pascal repeatedly destroys a position and then its negation: showing both that popular opinions are foolish and that they are sound, then undermining that corrective, illustrating the complexity of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological point underpins many fragments: accept the mixing of truth and falsity and be wary of dogmatic certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human weakness explains many valuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Human frailty accounts for why certain pursuits are esteemed (e.g., playing the lute) despite seeming trivial; weakness causes us to value certain non-essential skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal treats many popular valuations as rooted in human tendencies rather than objective worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of kings founded on people's folly
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of rulers rests as much on the people's folly as on reason; what appears as greatness often has weakness at its base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political legitimacy combines rational and irrational elements, with the latter often more stable and secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect institutional formality (ceremony breeds esteem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitually seeing rulers with ceremonial trappings makes people attribute intrinsic grandeur to them even when seen alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: guards, drums, officers create a conditioned awe; people mistake habituated respect for natural character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical writings on politics as therapy for madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers who advise on politics do so to mitigate the madness of those who imagine themselves rulers; political treatises aim to shape and moderate wildly ambitious minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal compares writing politics to setting rules for a lunatic asylum: it's a pragmatic corrective rather than absolute truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny as desire for universal power beyond proper scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny is the attempt to impose a single mode of mastery everywhere (to want what can only be had in another form), confusing different merits and duties (fear to the strong, love to the pleasant, belief to the learned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal condemns attempts to demand inappropriate interpersonal duties from people who have different qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept praise by mere association without merit
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone points out that great men esteem another to complain against you, ask what merit they saw; esteem by association is not itself a reason for your esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal counsel: demand substantive grounds for praise rather than relying on name-dropping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lust and force as sources of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Human actions derive from two main sources: lust (voluntary actions) and force (involuntary ones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological binary underlies many social and moral phenomena discussed in the fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep private thoughts secret, speak like the people
rubrics_metrics.description: One should keep inner judgments to oneself while outwardly conforming with popular speech and appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pragmatic maxim: preserve inner skepticism or truth-claims but avoid social disruption by publicizing them imprudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of opinion according to light one possesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Different groups (people, semi-learned, learned, devout, perfect Christians) honor or despise rank for different reasons; opinions vary with the 'light' or perspective one occupies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maps how epistemic or moral vantage points produce systematic differences in judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought constitutes human greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: All human dignity consists in thought; man is a 'thinking reed'—physically weak but elevated by the capacity to think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal grounds moral and existential claims on the distinctiveness of human thought over brute strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weakness and miseries are evidence of human greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Man's misery (awareness of his wretchedness) paradoxically proves his greatness—only a being with thought can be conscious of misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This paradoxical claim recurs: self-awareness of weakness is both misfortune and a sign of dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue judged by ordinary life rather than extreme efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: The true strength of a man's virtue is measured by his ordinary conduct, not by rare heroic efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal warns against admiring occasional excesses of virtue (or valour) without seeing balance across life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of opposing vices sustains virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: We maintain virtue by the balancing of two opposed vices; remove one vice and one falls into the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral equilibrium, not extremism, is the condition for stable virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic extremes are impractical and foolish
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic claims that consistent wisdom is easy for all are naïve; profound spiritual efforts are intermittent and rare, not permanent states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal critiques philosophical systems that overgeneralize from occasional exemplars to universal prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sceptical method: write without order to show incapacity for order
rubrics_metrics.description: Pascal intentionally writes disordered thoughts to demonstrate the subject's incapacity for systematic order; apparent disorder is itself meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological rubric legitimizes fragmentary exposition as faithful to the limits of human reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction neither proves nor disproves truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Contradiction is not a reliable sign of falsity, nor the lack of contradiction a sign of truth; parts of things can be true and false simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epistemic humility: avoid overreliance on logical contradiction as sole arbiter of truth in human affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human ideas are fragile and easily disturbed
rubrics_metrics.description: Human thought is liable to be disturbed by trivial noises or distractions (a fly buzzing), which can impede judgment on important matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal uses this to caution against expecting perfect, uninterrupted reasoning from human agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and chance govern thought acquisition and retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory is necessary for reason, but thoughts come and go by chance—no art guarantees retention; writing may even remind one of having forgotten a thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical remarks on the fallibility of thought: write to capture fleeting ideas, but accept the inevitability of forgetfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scepticism strengthens religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Scepticism can serve religion by humbling proud reason and prompting reliance on revelation; likewise scepticism undermines certain vain human pretensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal argues that scepticism and faith can be complementary: doubt deflates proud reason and opens a place for religious humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority and mediocrity as social norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess and defect are both criticized as madness; nothing is good except mediocrity as given by the majority's settlement; greatness lies in preserving the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal endorses a cautious preference for moderation and the social norm as restraining extremes, while acknowledging limits of that doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pride compensates for human misery
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride counterbalances miseries: people either conceal their miseries or glory in knowing them; pride is a psychological mechanism that mitigates suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological observation explains many paradoxes in human behavior (e.g., boasting about fallenness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Glory is both human baseness and excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The pursuit of glory is the greatest baseness yet also the greatest mark of human excellence, because esteem from others is a deep, indelible human desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ambivalence captures the moral complexity of seeking public esteem: morally dubious but evidencing human distinctiveness.
